title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). Two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions) and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics. Confirmatory outcomes (archived artifacts) show complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). We present the preregistered methodology, the exact artifact‑grounded results, a diagnostic analysis explaining why the design choices produced a ceiling, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work shows LLMs can produce syntactically plausible configuration templates in benchmarks and testbeds, and separate research demonstrates that verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops and deterministic network verifiers reduce configuration errors in IaC and related domains. The operational safety question for agentic NetOps pipelines is end‑to‑end: how do generator variability, runtime verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, and rollback interact to affect safe‑deploy outcomes?

Research question. Under the preregistered benchmark semantics, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 paired tasks.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (2) exact, archived confirmatory results showing universal acceptance of shared generator outputs by the deterministic validator (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0); (3) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis showing that shared_initial_generation combined with reusing a single deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling that makes the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interactions; and (4) concrete, artifact‑grounded benchmark‑hardening recommendations for future confirmatory runs.
sections.related_work: This study combines three research strands. First, intent→configuration generation: recent work demonstrates that LLMs can synthesize network configuration templates and intent translations in curated benchmarks and testbeds [1], [2], [3]. Second, verifier‑guided workflows and verifier‑guided fine‑tuning (e.g., verifier feedback for IaC) report correctness gains in infrastructure provisioning contexts and motivate analogous runtime guard integrations for NetOps [4], [8]. Third, deterministic network verifiers and reachability tools (header‑space style and Kubernetes reachability) are effective at finding configuration errors in offline and emulated settings but differ in scope and modeling assumptions [5]. Finally, agentic/tool‑augmented LLM architectures expand AIOps functionality but introduce new failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tool use) that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments [6], [7]. Surveys repeatedly note an evaluation gap: community‑standard, action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance are limited; this motivates our compact action‑aware staging benchmark and preregistered paired design.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study was preregistered (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1). Primary confirmatory estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (two‑sided). Confirmatory analysis used a permutation‑based paired difference test (paired_binary_analysis_v1); an exact McNemar two‑sided test was reported for corroboration. Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary outcomes.

Adapter semantics and shared generation. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. The preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): each task provoked a single deterministic LLM generation delivered identically to both baseline and guarded episodes. This choice isolates the validator’s acceptance decision on identical generator outputs rather than exposing independent generator variance between conditions; model_calls_used = 400 while planned episodes = 800.

Episode flow, validator policy, and repair rules. For each task the adapter requested one shared candidate from gpt‑5‑mini, delivered that candidate to both episodes, and in the guarded episode routed it to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied full intent‑constraint validation. The preregistered repair policy permitted up to one repair attempt in the guarded episode; repair_applied flags and validator_trace records were archived. Deterministic three‑replay consistency checks were required; pairs failing replay or encountering simulator errors would be excluded per the preregistration missingness_plan.

Confirmatory analysis. Primary analysis used exact permutation on paired safe‑deploy booleans (α=0.05); exact McNemar corroboration and paired bootstrap CI for the primary difference were computed. Sensitivity analyses were preregistered to treat excluded pairs as failures or to restrict permutations, but no exclusions occurred in this run.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. Run started 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation); complete_pairs = 400. Deterministic three‑replay checks passed for all pairs; no exclusions were recorded.

Primary confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). Baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0); guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency: n_11 = 400; n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0. Observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). These values are reproduced from the archived analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; see execution manifest).

Repair and rollback. repair_applied = false across all 800 episodes; no rollbacks invoked. Validator traces show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations, which explains universal acceptance: when the shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5, both conditions recorded safe‑deploy.

Aggregated task difficulty summary (required revision). We computed difficulty counts and percentages from the archived per‑task difficulty labels in execution/task_manifest.jsonl (artifact path and manifest SHA‑256 referenced in the execution manifest). Aggregated counts: medium = 100 tasks (25.0%), hard = 150 tasks (37.5%), very_hard = 150 tasks (37.5%). Table 1 summarizes these counts and percentages and cites execution/task_manifest.jsonl for auditors to verify. (The manifest contains full per‑task difficulty metadata for N=400 pairs.)

Statistical interpretation. The observed deterministic ceiling collapses inferential variance: exact tests report p = 1.0, but these statistics do not provide evidence about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics because the design prevented the guard from having an opportunity to intervene. The preregistered power calculation assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and within‑pair variability sufficient to detect ≈0.10 absolute difference with N=400; those assumptions are invalidated by the observed ceiling and thus the original power rationale does not apply to these results.
sections.discussion:
Cause of the uninformative primary estimand. Two preregistered design choices produced the deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation intentionally removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When the deterministic validator accepts the shared candidate, both conditions necessarily record identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference must be zero. This is a construct‑validity consequence of the frozen design, not evidence that runtime verification lacks value in general.

Consequences and recommendations. Because the observed ceiling invalidates the preregistered power rationale, permutation/McNemar p‑values of 1.0 correctly reflect the data but cannot adjudicate whether a runtime guard would have improved outcomes under an alternative design. From archived validator_trace and execution manifests we propose concrete, artifact‑grounded benchmark hardening steps:

1) Use independent_condition_generation = true so each condition receives independently sampled generator outputs and the guard has opportunities to accept/block/request repair.
2) Use distinct runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer implementations (or a held‑out scorer) to avoid conflating runtime acceptance with analysis scoring.
3) Preregister controlled perturbation seeds (adversarial seeding) to guarantee nontrivial baseline failure rates for power preservation; the task generator supports deterministic seeding.
4) Difficulty‑stratified sampling to ensure a sufficient fraction of very_hard tasks to produce measurable baseline errors; per‑task difficulty labels are archived and can be deterministically sampled.
5) Instrument and preregister repair/rollback metrics (repair counts, repairs applied, time‑to‑rollback) which the validator_trace schema already records.

Operational implication. Experiments that remove generator variance hide potential benefits of runtime guards; to evaluate guards, preserve generator variance and use independent adjudication channels.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on an action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect resulted from frozen design and implementation homogeneity and rendered the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations above are implementable directly from the archived manifests and validator traces and will preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for follow‑on preregistered work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl (manifest SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest) and can be audited; Table 1 reports aggregated counts and percentages computed from that manifest.
